questions.question: The chart shows the closing cash balance for each month once the forecast has been completed, together with the existing overdraft limit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the cash-flow forecast by calculating the closing balance for each of the six months, and identify the month in which the forecast reaches its lowest closing balance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate by how much the forecast breaches the existing overdraft limit, and state the month in which the breach is deepest.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The finance director proposes to bring 8 000 of the receipts expected in April forward into March, by offering customers a discount for early payment. Revise the forecast to show the effect of this proposal, and evaluate whether it removes the breach of the overdraft limit.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why no re-timing of receipts or payments within January to April can remove the breach, and recommend one action that would remove it. Support your recommendation with figures.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Each month's closing balance is its opening balance plus the receipts of that month less the payments of that month, and the opening balance of each month is the closing balance of the month before (M1). January opens at 12 000 and closes at $12 + 20 - 24 = 8\,000$; February opens at 8 000 and closes at $8 + 18 - 23 = 3\,000$; March opens at 3 000 and closes at $3 + 14 - 26 = -9\,000$; April opens at minus 9 000 and closes at $-9 + 16 - 13 = -6\,000$; May opens at minus 6 000 and closes at $-6 + 22 - 13 = 3\,000$; and June opens at 3 000 and closes at $3 + 26 - 15 = 14\,000$ (A1). The closing balances are therefore 8, 3, minus 9, minus 6, 3 and 14 thousand, and the lowest of them is minus 9 000 in March (A1). It is worth noting that the business recovers by May with no action at all, which is why this is a liquidity problem rather than a solvency one: the cash is arriving late rather than not arriving, and the question is only whether the business can survive the gap.

**(b)** The existing limit is minus 5 000, so the March closing balance of minus 9 000 breaches it by $9\,000 - 5\,000 = 4\,000$ (M1)(A1). March is the month in which the breach is deepest, but it is not the only one: the April balance of minus 6 000 breaches the same limit by 1 000, so the facility is exceeded in two consecutive months.

**(c)** Bringing 8 000 of April's receipts into March raises March's receipts from 14 000 to 22 000 and reduces April's from 16 000 to 8 000, leaving the total for the two months unchanged at 30 000 (M1). Re-chaining the balances gives 8, 3, minus 1, minus 6, 3 and 14 thousand (A1). The lowest balance is now minus 6 000, in April, so the breach has been reduced from 4 000 to 1 000 but has not been removed (A1). The proposal therefore fails, and the reason is structural rather than arithmetic. The closing balance at the end of April is the opening balance of 12 000 plus the receipts of the first four months less the payments of the first four months, that is $12 + 68 - 86 = -6$, and that expression contains no reference to which month any receipt falls in, so moving a receipt from April to March cannot change it (A1). The discount also carries a cost the director has not counted: paying 8 000 early in return for a discount of, say, two per cent reduces the cash actually received by about 160, so the position after the proposal is slightly worse than the figures above show.

**(d)** Any re-timing of receipts or payments inside January to April changes when cash arrives but not how much cash the window contains, and the closing balance at the end of April is fixed by that total (M1). Delaying a March payment into April has exactly the same effect as bringing an April receipt into March: the March balance improves and the April balance gives the improvement back, so the deficit moves rather than closes, and the best that re-timing can achieve is a lowest balance of minus 6 000, which is still a breach of 1 000 (A1). What would work is permanent cash arriving before the trough. A loan or a capital injection of 4 000 received in January raises every later closing balance by 4 000 and gives 12, 7, minus 5, minus 2, 7 and 18 thousand, whose lowest balance of minus 5 000 sits exactly on the limit (A1). Extending the overdraft facility to 9 000 would achieve the same result by changing the constraint rather than the cash, and a permanent reduction of 4 000 in payments, for example by renegotiating the March payment run, would achieve it by raising the cumulative total. The one option that is not available is to reschedule inside the window, because the total the window contains is already fixed.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for the method of chaining opening balance, receipts and payments, (A1)(A1) for the six closing balances and the identification of March. Accept a candidate who shows the balances as a running total rather than in a table. A candidate who computes receipts minus payments without carrying the opening balance forward obtains 4, 5, 12, 3, 9 and 11 and scores no marks: the whole point of the part is that the opening balance of each month is the previous closing balance.
(b) (M1) for comparing the lowest balance with the limit, (A1) for 4 000 and March. Accept 'exceeds the limit by 4 000' without the month, provided the month is named somewhere in the part. Follow-through applies from (a).
(c) (M1) for the revised receipts, (A1) for the revised balances, (A1) for the conclusion that the breach is not removed, (A1) for the reason. The reason must be about the invariance of the cumulative total, not merely an assertion that the deficit has moved: a candidate who says only that 'the problem now happens in April' scores (A1) for the conclusion and no mark for the reason. Accept a candidate who reaches minus 6 000 by any correct route.
(d) (M1) for the statement that re-timing cannot change the total cash in the window, (A1) for the numerical consequence, that the best achievable balance is minus 6 000, (A1) for a workable recommendation supported by figures. Accept any of the three routes named in the answer, and accept a candidate who recommends deferring a payment beyond April provided the figures are given. A recommendation with no figures scores (M1) at most.
questions.explanation:
The item is built so that the remedy a student reaches for first is arithmetically insufficient, and the reason it is insufficient is the concept the topic is about. A cash-flow forecast is a statement about the *timing* of cash, and it is natural to conclude that a timing problem has a timing solution. Here it does not. The closing balance at the end of April is the opening balance plus the receipts of four months less the payments of four months, and no rearrangement of when within those four months the cash arrives can change that total. Re-timing moves the trough from March to April and shrinks it from 4 000 to 1 000; it cannot remove it.

That the trough is capped is worth stating precisely, because it is what makes the evaluation decisive rather than a matter of opinion. Whatever fraction of April's receipts is brought into March, and whatever fraction of March's payments is pushed into April, the April closing balance stays at minus 6 000. The cap is a property of the forecast, not of the particular proposal, and a candidate who tests only the proposal the director suggests will find the improvement and may stop there. The part that earns the marks is the one that asks whether the improvement is enough.

The chart carries the part of the argument that a table cannot. In the table the trough is a single negative number among positives; on the chart the two red bars below the dashed limit line show at a glance that the problem is not one bad month but two, and that the second one is created by the proposal that was meant to solve the first. Reading a forecast off its chart is the skill the paper is modelling, and it is the reason the figure is here rather than the table alone.

The final part asks for a recommendation that works, and the simplest is a loan or capital injection of 4 000 received before the trough, which raises every later balance by that amount and lands the lowest balance exactly on the limit. A candidate may instead extend the facility to 9 000, or take 4 000 out of the March payment run. All three are accepted, and all three share the property that the re-timing proposals lack: they change the cumulative cash in the window rather than its distribution.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Compute the six closing balances, find the negative one, and treat the shortfall as a timing problem by bringing the following month's receipts forward into the month with the deficit, on the reasoning that the business is short of cash in one month rather than short of cash overall.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The proposal addresses the month rather than the cumulative position. The closing balance at the end of the fourth month is the opening balance plus the receipts of four months less the payments of four months, a quantity that contains no information about which month any receipt falls in, so the improvement in the worst month is exactly cancelled by the deterioration in the month the cash was taken from and the deficit survives in a new place.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The evaluation concludes that the proposal succeeds because the March balance rises from minus 9 000 to minus 1 000 and the largest deficit is smaller, when the April balance has fallen to minus 6 000 and the limit is still breached.

verification.method: Every balance was recomputed in Python, and the chaining of each opening balance to the previous closing balance was asserted rather than assumed. The proposal was tested at several sizes of transfer, from zero to 10 000, and the April closing balance was confirmed to remain at minus 6 000 for every one of them; delaying March payments into April was tested separately and found to leave the same balance fixed. The identity 12 + 68 - 86 = -6 was checked against the four-month sums, and the loan alternative was tested at 3 000, which still breaches, and at 4 000, which does not. The figure draws the bars and the limit line from the same balances.
solution_skeleton: chain the opening balance of each month to the closing balance of the previous month
identify the lowest closing balance and compare it with the limit
revise the receipts for the two months affected by the proposal and re-chain
test whether the revised lowest balance clears the limit
show that the closing balance at the end of the fourth month is fixed by the four-month totals
propose an action that changes the cumulative cash rather than its timing, and check the revised balances against the limit

questions.challenge_mechanism: The contract earns a positive contribution of £7 a unit, so the obvious test says accept it. But the contract is also the only reason output crosses 6 000 units, and crossing that line costs £18 000 a month whether the contract is for one unit above the line or for four thousand. The decision therefore turns on a threshold the student has to locate: contribution must cover the step, and between the step and the point where it does, the business is worse off than it was before the contract existed.
questions.question: The graph shows Kestrel's monthly profit plotted against the size of the contract. Answer every part with reference to the relevant range, and give money answers to the nearest pound and output answers to the nearest whole unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per unit at the current selling price, the monthly break-even output, and Kestrel's current monthly profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the contribution per unit on the contract, and Kestrel's monthly profit if a contract for 2 500 units per month is accepted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the range of contract sizes, if any, for which accepting the contract would leave Kestrel with a lower monthly profit than it earns now, and determine the smallest contract size at which crossing into the second shift becomes worthwhile.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The retailer's final offer is 2 500 units per month for one year. Evaluate the finance director's claim that the contract must be accepted because every unit adds to contribution, and recommend one change to the terms that would make the contract worth accepting.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Contribution per unit at the current price is £25 − £13 = £12 (A1). Break-even output is fixed costs divided by the contribution per unit, £48 000 ÷ £12 = 4 000 units per month (M1)(A1). Current output is exactly 4 000 units, so the current monthly profit is 4 000 × £12 − £48 000 = £0: the business is precisely at break-even.
**(b)** On the contract the price is £20, so the contribution per unit is £20 − £13 = £7 (A1). A contract of 2 500 units takes total output to 4 000 + 2 500 = 6 500 units, which is above the 6 000-unit ceiling of the first shift, so fixed costs rise to £48 000 + £18 000 = £66 000 (M1). Total contribution is 4 000 × £12 + 2 500 × £7 = £48 000 + £17 500 = £65 500, so the monthly profit becomes £65 500 − £66 000 = −£500 (A1). Kestrel would move from breaking even to losing £500 a month.
**(c)** Let q be the contract size. While 4 000 + q ≤ 6 000, that is q ≤ 2 000, no second shift is needed and profit is 7q, which is positive for every q > 0 (M1). Once q > 2 000 the extra £18 000 of fixed cost is incurred, so profit is 7q − 18 000, which is negative for q < 18 000 ÷ 7 = 2 571.43, that is up to and including 2 571 units (M1)(A1). The contract therefore leaves Kestrel worse off than it is now for every size from 2 001 to 2 571 units inclusive (A1), and the smallest size at which the step repays its own cost is 2 572 units, where profit is 7 × 2 572 − 18 000 = £4 (A1). Profit is not monotonic in the size of the contract: 2 000 units earns £14 000, 2 001 units loses £3 993, and 2 572 units earns £4.
**(d)** The director's claim is true of the unit and false of the decision. Each contract unit does add £7, but the relevant comparison is not between £7 and zero; it is between the £17 500 the contract contributes and the £18 000 of fixed cost that exists only because the contract was taken (M1). At 2 500 units the contract therefore reduces profit from £0 to −£500 a month, and because the contract runs for a year the loss is about −£6 000 over its life, before any allowance for the disruption of running a second shift for twelve months (A1). Two things qualify this. First, the arithmetic is knife-edge: a loss of £500 a month is 0.8% of monthly contribution, so a small change in the terms reverses the answer, and the business may rationally accept a marginal loss to secure a national listing (A1). Second, the loss is a property of the size and not of the idea: the contract is profitable below 2 001 units and above 2 571 units. The recommendation is to renegotiate one of the two (M1). At 2 500 units the contribution per unit must satisfy 2 500c ≥ 18 000, so c ≥ £7.20 and the price must be at least £20.20; alternatively the contract should be capped at 2 000 units or raised to at least 2 572 units (A1).
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (A1) for £12, (M1) for dividing fixed costs by contribution, (A1) for 4 000 units and £0. Accept break-even quoted as £100 000 of revenue if the unit figure accompanies it.
(b) (A1) for £7, (M1) for noticing that 6 500 units exceeds the 6 000-unit ceiling and adding £18 000, (A1) for −£500. A candidate who computes £17 500 of contribution and ignores the step scores at most one of the three; this is the whole item, so do not award follow-through from it.
(c) (M1) for treating the two ranges separately, (M1) for solving 7q ≥ 18 000, (A1) for the closed range 2 001 to 2 571 units, (A1) for 2 572 units. Accept 2 571.4 units quoted as the break-even size provided the candidate then rounds *up* to 2 572 for the smallest whole-unit size; a candidate who rounds down to 2 571 has not answered the question and loses the final mark.
(d) (M1) for comparing £17 500 with £18 000 rather than with zero, (A1) for the conclusion that the contract as offered reduces profit, (A1) for a developed qualitative point such as the twelve-month commitment or the strategic value of the listing, (M1)(A1) for a recommendation supported by a figure — £20.20, 2 000 units or 2 572 units. Do not credit 'accept because contribution is positive' however well argued; the question asks for an evaluation of that claim, not a restatement of it.
questions.explanation:
The item is built around a quantity that the syllabus names but that questions almost never test: the relevant range. Break-even analysis is linear inside one range and stops being linear at its edge, and the standard classroom treatment of a special order asks only whether the order's contribution is positive. Here it is, and the order is still wrong, because the order is also the cause of a step in fixed costs that no unit-level calculation can see.

The structure is chosen so that the obvious remedy and the correct remedy are different in kind. A candidate who reaches for contribution answers (b) as £17 500 and stops. The candidate has to discover the step, then discover that the step is caused by the decision rather than merely coincident with it, and then discover the shape of the result: profit is discontinuous at 2 000 units and *rises* again afterwards, so both 'small enough to stay on one shift' and 'large enough to pay for the second' are correct answers and the sizes between them are the only wrong ones. That is a genuinely different task from computing a break-even output, and it is the task a manager actually faces when a large customer's order arrives.

Part (d) is not decoration. stimulus.title: Northgate Leisure: the climbing wall survey
stimulus.body:
Northgate Leisure runs a leisure centre with 400 members. It is deciding whether to build a climbing wall, and posts a questionnaire to all of them asking whether they would use it.

The membership has two segments. There are 100 premium members, who pay a higher monthly fee and visit at least twice a week, and 300 standard members, who pay the basic fee. Of the 100 premium members, 80 return the questionnaire. Of the 300 standard members, 90 return it.

Among the 80 premium respondents, 56 say they would use the climbing wall. Among the 90 standard respondents, 36 say they would use it. The marketing manager writes in her report that a majority of members want the climbing wall, and recommends that the board approve it.

questions.challenge_mechanism: The pooled sample of 170 is not 170 members; it is 80 of the 100 people who care most about the centre and 90 of the 300 who do not, so every premium reply stands for one and a quarter members while every standard reply stands for three and a third. Because the two segments disagree by thirty percentage points, the population figure has to be rebuilt from the two segment readings and their known sizes, and it lands on the other side of fifty per cent from the pooled sample.
questions.question: The chart compares the composition of the membership with the composition of the achieved sample. Use the data to answer the following.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the response rate for each segment and for the survey as a whole, and use them to show that the achieved sample is not representative of the membership.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of all respondents who said they would use the climbing wall, and state the conclusion the marketing manager draws from it.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the known size of each segment, determine a weighted estimate of the percentage of all 400 members who would use the wall, and hence estimate how many members that is. Explain why this figure differs from the one in part (b), and why the direction of the difference could have been predicted before any calculation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate the marketing manager's claim that a majority of members want the climbing wall, and recommend how Northgate should have run or reported the survey so that the claim could be tested.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Premium response rate: 80 ÷ 100 = 80%. Standard response rate: 90 ÷ 300 = 30%. Overall: 170 ÷ 400 = 42.5% (M1)(A1). Premium members are a quarter of the membership, 100 ÷ 400 = 25%, but they are 80 of the 170 responses, which is 47.1% of the achieved sample (A1). A sample in which one segment is represented at nearly twice its true weight is not representative, and the cause is visible in the response rates: premium members were more than two and a half times as likely to reply.
**(b)** Of the 170 responses, 56 + 36 = 92 said they would use the wall, so the pooled figure is 92 ÷ 170 = 54.1% (M1)(A1). The manager concludes that a majority — more than half — of members want the climbing wall, and recommends approval (A1).
**(c)** Weight each segment's approval rate by its share of the membership. Premium approval is 56 ÷ 80 = 70% and standard approval is 36 ÷ 90 = 40%. The weighted estimate is 0.25 × 70% + 0.75 × 40% = 17.5% + 30% = 47.5% (M1)(A1), which is 0.475 × 400 = 190 of the 400 members (A1). The pooled figure is higher because the sample contains too many premium members, and premium members are the segment that wants the wall most: 70% against 40%, a gap of thirty percentage points. The direction of the error was predictable before any arithmetic, because the segment with the higher response rate is also the segment with the higher approval rate, so self-selection must inflate the pooled answer (A1).
**(d)** The claim is not supported. The weighted estimate is 47.5%, which is below half, and 190 of 400 members is 10 short of a majority (M1). Two things qualify this. First, 47.5% is itself an estimate resting on the assumption that non-respondents in each segment resemble respondents in that segment — an assumption the data cannot test, and one that is least safe here, since people who did not bother to answer a questionnaire about a climbing wall may be people who do not want a climbing wall (A1). Second, the commercial case may not need a majority: if premium members generate most of the revenue and 70% of them want the wall, the board might rationally build it anyway (A1). The recommendation is to re-run the survey so that the answer can be tested rather than assumed: weight the responses, or use quota sampling with a target of 100 premium and 300 standard members, follow up non-respondents, and report the result by segment with the response rate stated alongside it (M1)(A1).
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for a correct response rate calculation in any of the three forms, (A1) for all three rates correct, (A1) for the comparison of 25% of the membership with 47.1% of the sample. A candidate who says the sample is unrepresentative because only 42.5% replied, without comparing the two segments, has identified a real but different problem: credit it only if the segment comparison is also attempted.
(b) (M1) for 92 of 170, (A1) for 54.1%, (A1) for stating the manager's conclusion. The conclusion must be reported faithfully even though it is wrong; the evaluation comes in (d).
(c) (M1) for weighting by membership shares rather than by response counts, (A1) for 70% and 40%, (A1) for 47.5% and 190 members, (A1) for the direction argument — the segment that responds more also approves more, so the pooled figure must be too high. Credit an equivalent argument carried out in counts rather than percentages.
(d) (M1) for the conclusion that the claim is not supported, with the weighted figure used, (A1) for the point that non-respondents are unobserved and may differ, (A1) for a second developed consideration such as revenue weighting by segment, and (M1)(A1) for a recommendation that would let the claim be tested — quota sampling, follow-up of non-respondents, or reporting response rates and segment breakdowns. Do not credit 'the sample is too small' on its own: 170 responses is a large sample; the problem is which 170.
questions.explanation:
The item attacks the most common error in the market research topic, which is not a calculation error at all. Students are taught that a bigger sample is a better sample, and a sample of 170 from a population of 400 looks excellent: it is 42.5% of every member. The error is invisible in the pooled figures and appears the moment the sample is split by segment.

The design makes the two errors point the same way on purpose. Non-response is only a bias if the people who do not answer differ from those who do, so the item gives the student the means to see that difference (80% against 30%) and a payoff for seeing it (70% against 40%). The population figure is then recoverable from two aggregate readings — the two segment approval rates — combined with the known segment sizes, and it falls on the other side of the majority line the manager claimed. Recovering a whole from weighted parts is the actual skill, and it is the one a manager needs when a survey comes back looking decisive.

Part (d) keeps the item honest. The weighted estimate is still an assumption about people who did not answer, so the correct conclusion is that the manager's claim is unproven rather than false — a distinction that matters more, in practice, than the arithmetic that precedes it.

Here the naming is not enough: the item supplies the segment sizes and the segment counts so that the direction and the size of the bias have to be computed, and it is arranged so that the pooled result and the weighted result fall on opposite sides of the majority the manager claimed. The business decision is then attached to the corrected figure rather than to the raw one.

difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The 170 responses are not 170 members drawn from the membership. questions.challenge_mechanism: Grouped-data questions always ask for an estimated mean, and the routine is to take midpoints. Here the final class has no upper end, so it has no midpoint: whatever value the student substitutes is an assumption about six named people, and because those six are the ones with the longest absences, changing the assumption alone can push the mean above any number. The mean is therefore not merely inaccurate but underivable, while the median and quartiles are fixed by position alone and survive unchanged.
questions.question: The histogram shows the same distribution, with the open-ended final class drawn as a faded bar. Use the n/2 convention for the median and quartiles of a grouped distribution, and give all answers to two decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Reproduce the HR director's estimate of the mean from the grouped table, stating the assumption you have to make about the final class in order to produce it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the median and the interquartile range of the distribution, and state what assumption, if any, the open-ended class forces you to make in order to find them.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that no upper bound can be placed on the mean from this table, and determine the greatest lower bound that the table does guarantee.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate the HR director's claim that the mean absence is 5.71 days and that the six-day target has been met, and recommend how absence should be reported instead.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Using midpoints 1, 4, 7 and 10 for the first four classes and assuming the last class has the same width as the others, so a midpoint of 13 (M1), the estimated mean is (14 × 1 + 23 × 4 + 18 × 7 + 9 × 10 + 6 × 13) ÷ 70 = (14 + 92 + 126 + 90 + 78) ÷ 70 = 400 ÷ 70 = 5.71 days (A1). The assumption is that the six employees in the open class were each absent for about 13 days; nothing in the table supports it, and the class was left open precisely because those six records were not broken down (A1).
**(b)** With 70 employees the median is the 35th value. Cumulative frequencies are 14, 37, 55, 64 and 70, so the 35th value lies in the class 3 – 5, whose lower boundary is 2.5 and whose width is 3: median = 2.5 + ((35 − 14) ÷ 23) × 3 = 2.5 + 2.74 = 5.24 days (M1)(A1). The lower quartile is the 17.5th value, also in 3 – 5: 2.5 + ((17.5 − 14) ÷ 23) × 3 = 2.96 days. The upper quartile is the 52.5th value, in 6 – 8: 5.5 + ((52.5 − 37) ÷ 18) × 3 = 8.08 days. The interquartile range is 8.08 − 2.96 = 5.13 days (A1). No assumption is needed: these are positional measures, and the six employees in the open class affect them only by standing above them in the ordering.
**(c)** The six employees in the final class each have at least 12 days, but the table places no ceiling on them. If they each had 60 days, the mean would be (14 + 92 + 126 + 90 + 6 × 60) ÷ 70 = 682 ÷ 70 = 9.74 days (M1); if they each had 200 days it would be 21.74 days (A1). Since the assumed value can be increased without limit, no upper bound on the mean can be derived from the table (A1). The smallest the mean can be is when all six are at the foot of their class, 12 days: (14 + 92 + 126 + 90 + 72) ÷ 70 = 394 ÷ 70 = 5.63 days, so the table guarantees only that the mean is at least 5.63 days (A1).
**(d)** The claim is unsound in two ways. The figure of 5.71 days is not an estimate of the mean at all: it is the value obtained when the six longest absences are each assumed to be 13 days, and the same table is consistent with a mean of 9.74 days or of 21 days, so the mean cannot be compared with the target (M1)(A1). What the table does support is a different statement: the median is 5.24 days and therefore below the target, 8.6% of the workforce (6 of 70) were absent for at least 12 days, and the distribution is right-skewed with an interquartile range of 5.13 days — so the typical employee is comfortably inside the target and a small group is far outside it (A1). The recommendation is to report absence with positional measures and the tail: the median, the interquartile range and the percentage of employees above a threshold such as twelve days, together with the exact figures for the six long-term cases, which the HR department already holds (M1)(A1).

(a) (M1) for using midpoints at all, (A1) for 5.71 days, (A1) for naming the assumption explicitly. A candidate who writes 5.71 with no comment on the open class earns the method mark only; the point of the part is that the number carries an invisible assumption.
(b) (M1) for locating the median class by cumulative frequency, (A1) for 5.24 days, (A1) for the quartiles and the interquartile range of 5.13 days. Accept quartile positions of (n+1)/4 and 3(n+1)/4 if applied consistently, with quartiles of 2.99 and 8.21 and an IQR of 5.22; do not penalise the alternative convention, but do penalise a candidate who mixes them. The statement that no assumption is required is worth credit here even if it is not separately marked.
(c) (M1) for substituting a large value into the open class, (A1) for a second such value or for a general argument, (A1) for the conclusion that no upper bound exists, (A1) for the lower bound of 5.63 days. The lower bound must use 12, the smallest value the class permits; a candidate who uses 11.5 has misread the class and loses this mark.
(d) (M1) for distinguishing an estimate that depends on the assumption from one that does not, (A1) for the conclusion that the claim cannot be tested from the mean, (A1) for the supportable statements — median 5.24, 8.6% at twelve days or more — and (M1)(A1) for a reporting recommendation. Do not credit 'collect better data' on its own: the data already exist, and the fault is in the summary chosen.
questions.explanation:
Every grouped-data question a student meets asks for an estimated mean, and the method — midpoint times frequency, summed and divided — becomes a reflex. This item is built so that the reflex produces a number that looks exactly like the right kind of answer and cannot be right, because one of the inputs does not exist.

The open-ended class is doing two jobs. Mechanically, it removes the midpoint, so the mean is not approximate but underivable, and the student has to say what the table still guarantees instead — a one-sided bound. Conceptually, it removes the *wrong* summary from the board's hands: the six employees who caused the class to be left open are the ones the business needs to manage, and the mean is the one statistic that lets them disappear into an average. The median and the interquartile range are unaffected by how large their values are, which is precisely why they are the right measures for a skewed distribution with a long tail.

The judgement in (d) is therefore not an add-on. A student who simply reports that the target is unmet has missed the more useful finding: the typical employee is well inside the target, 8.6% are far outside it, and those are different problems requiring different responses. Reporting the median does not conceal those six cases: it reports them as a percentage of the workforce rather than averaging them into a figure that no longer describes anybody, which is what the board's target actually needs.

The business setting is added so that the choice between the mean and the median has a consequence — a target that is met or not met — rather than being a preference.

questions.syllabus_ref: Unit 3: 3.8 Investment appraisal (payback period, the net present value method and the criteria used to choose between projects); 3.2 Sources of finance
questions.subtopic: 3.8 Capital rationing: the constraint binds only in combination, so the project with the highest net present value is not the one to choose

stimulus.title: Verrano Marine Ltd: three projects and a capital limit
stimulus.body:
Verrano Marine Ltd builds small electric boats. The board has approved £120 000 of capital for new equipment this year and has decided that no further funds will be available for twelve months. Three projects have been appraised. Each is indivisible: it must be undertaken in full or not at all, and no project can be started in part.

All three net present values have been calculated using a cost of capital of 10% and the discount factors supplied with the appraisal. The finance director recommends Project A, on the grounds that it has the highest net present value of the three.

questions.challenge_mechanism: The capital limit is not breached by any single project, so it looks as though the choice is simply the best project. It binds only in combination: once A is chosen, the £20 000 left over is too small to fund anything, and the two projects that would together earn most of the available net present value are the two the director ranked second and third. The student has to enumerate the combinations before ranking them, because the ranking of single projects and the ranking of feasible combinations are different orderings of the same three items.
questions.question: The board must choose a combination of projects that fits inside the £120 000 limit. Answer every part, giving money to the nearest pound and ratios to three decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value earned per £1 invested for each project, and rank the three projects by that measure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine every combination of projects that fits inside the £120 000 limit, and the total net present value of each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the combination Verrano should choose, and calculate the net present value forgone if the finance director's recommendation to take Project A is followed. State how much of the £120 000 would be left unspent in each case.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate the decision to select the two smaller projects rather than Project A, considering at least one further financial factor and two non-financial factors.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Net present value per £1 invested: A, £40 000 ÷ £100 000 = £0.400; B, £25 000 ÷ £40 000 = £0.625; C, £34 000 ÷ £80 000 = £0.425 (M1)(A1). Ranked by this measure the order is B, then C, then A — the reverse of the ranking by net present value alone (A1).
**(b)** The combinations that fit inside £120 000 are: A alone, £100 000, £40 000; B alone, £40 000, £25 000; C alone, £80 000, £34 000; and B together with C, £120 000, £59 000 (M1)(A1). A with B would cost £140 000 and A with C £180 000, and all three would cost £220 000, so none of those is possible; the projects are indivisible, so no part of A can be funded with the money left after B (A1).
**(c)** The best combination is B together with C, with a total net present value of £59 000, which also uses the whole of the £120 000 (M1). If the finance director's recommendation is followed, Verrano takes A alone and earns £40 000, so the net present value forgone is £59 000 − £40 000 = £19 000 (A1). Taking A leaves £120 000 − £100 000 = £20 000 unspent, which is less than the £40 000 that B needs and less than the £80 000 that C needs, so the balance earns nothing (M1); taking B and C leaves £120 000 − £120 000 = £0 unspent (A1).
**(d)** The financial case is straightforward but narrower than it looks: the ranking by net present value per £1 is the right ranking only while capital is rationed, and it says B then C, which is also the best feasible combination (M1). A further financial factor is risk over time: B and C pay back in 1.8 and 2.6 years against 3.4 years for A, so the chosen combination returns the cash well inside the twelve months in which no further funds are available, and leaves the business able to re-appraise A next year with real cash rather than with borrowed money (A1). Against that, two non-financial factors pull the other way. Committing the whole £120 000 leaves no contingency: if C overruns, there is no reserve, whereas A leaves £20 000 unused and some flexibility (A1). And A is the hull moulding line, which is the strategic asset — it raises capacity for the whole product range and may be the project that a competitor could not copy, while a test rig and a set of jigs improve quality and fit-out rather than the product itself (A1).
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for dividing each net present value by its own investment, (A1) for all three ratios correct to three decimal places, (A1) for the ranking B, C, A. A candidate who ranks by net present value per £1 but then selects on the same basis without checking feasibility has only completed half of the method: the ratios rank projects, they do not by themselves produce a feasible set.
(b) (M1) for testing combinations rather than single projects, (A1) for the four feasible sets with their totals, (A1) for showing why A with B and A with C are excluded — the cost, not a preference. Credit a candidate who lists all seven subsets provided the infeasible ones are identified as such.
(c) (M1) for identifying B and C, (A1) for £19 000, (M1) for the £20 000 balance and the observation that it funds nothing, (A1) for the £0 balance on the chosen combination. Follow-through applies from an arithmetic slip in the ratios but not from a failure to test combinations at all.
(d) Accept any two developed non-financial factors; the ones named in the answer are contingency and strategic fit, and credit should also go to quality, staff skills, flexibility, or the effect on next year's capital budget. Do not credit 'A has the highest net present value' as an argument here: that is the recommendation under evaluation, and repeating it is not an evaluation.
questions.explanation:
Investment appraisal is taught project by project, and the decision rule that survives in students' notes is 'choose the highest net present value'. That rule is correct when capital is unlimited and wrong the moment it is not, and the two settings produce different orderings of the very same three projects. This item exists to make the difference visible and computable.

The structure is deliberately unhelpful to the obvious answer. Project A has the largest net present value, so the director's recommendation looks considered; it also leaves £20 000 idle, and the item is arranged so that the leftover is too small to fund the second-best project, which is what makes the mistake expensive rather than merely inefficient. The student has to enumerate what is feasible before ranking at all, and the answer to (c) — £19 000 forgone — is the price of skipping that step.

Part (d) stops the item from implying that the arithmetic settles everything. The chosen pair uses every pound and has the shortest paybacks, which cuts both ways: there is no contingency left, and the project with the strategic content is the one deferred. A student who can hold both of those at once has done the evaluation the syllabus asks for. Capital rationing is also temporary: if the limit lifts in twelve months the correct statement is that Project A is deferred rather than rejected, and the appraisal should be repeated next year against the cash the chosen projects will by then have returned.

provenance.adaptation: The source genre supplies two or three projects and asks which should be chosen, usually with capital available for all of them, so the ranking by net present value is decisive. Here a limit is imposed that no single project breaches, which is exactly the case in which the limit is easy to overlook: the item asks for the feasible combinations explicitly, and the numbers are chosen so that the highest-value single project is not in the best feasible set and leaves a balance too small to fund anything else.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Rank the projects by net present value, take the one at the top of the list, and note that the £20 000 left over is a pity but does not change the decision.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The capital limit does not bind on any single project, which is why it is invisible; it binds on pairs. Once A is taken the remaining £20 000 funds nothing, so the choice is not between three projects but between four feasible sets, and the best of those is the two projects the director ranked second and third.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The recommendation takes Project A because its net present value of £40 000 is the largest, and reports the £20 000 balance as unspent, when B together with C fits inside the same limit and earns £59 000 — £19 000 more.

verification.method: Every figure was recomputed in Python. All seven non-empty subsets of the three projects were enumerated and their total investment compared with the limit, giving exactly four feasible sets; the best of them was confirmed to be B with C by direct comparison rather than by the ratio ranking, since the ranking by net present value per £1 is only a heuristic under indivisibility. The leftover after A was checked against both remaining investments and is smaller than each. The opportunity cost was confirmed two ways, as £59 000 − £40 000 and as the sum of the two forgone net present values less nothing.
solution_skeleton: divide each project's net present value by the capital it consumes
list every combination of indivisible projects the limit permits
total the net present value of each feasible combination
pick the best feasible set rather than the best single project
value the director's choice against it as an opportunity cost

stimulus.title: Trentvale Components Ltd: three stages and two proposals
stimulus.body:
Trentvale Components Ltd makes a machined housing in three sequential stages. Cutting can process 100 units per hour and produces no scrap. Machining can process 90 units per hour, and 10% of the units it processes are scrapped and sold as swarf. Finishing can process 84 units per hour and produces no scrap. Every good unit that leaves finishing is sold immediately: demand is not a constraint, and the line runs for 40 hours a week for 48 weeks a year.

The housing sells for £40 and has a variable cost of £22, so each good unit contributes £18. Two proposals have been costed at £250 000 each.

Proposal 1 raises finishing capacity from 84 to 110 units per hour. Proposal 2 buys a better tool holder for machining, reducing the scrap rate there from 10% to 5%. The operations director argues that finishing must be extended first, because 84 units per hour is the lowest capacity in the factory.

questions.challenge_mechanism: Capacity is quoted per stage, and the smallest number looks like the constraint. It is not, because the scrap at machining is applied *before* the units reach finishing: machining delivers 81 good units an hour to a stage that could handle 84, so finishing is starved and has three units an hour of spare capacity while carrying the lowest stated number. The student has to convert each stage's nameplate capacity into good units delivered, and then price the error: the director's proposal buys zero extra output, and the same money spent on the scrap rate buys three units an hour immediately.
questions.question: The diagram shows the three stages with their stated capacities. Answer every part, giving output to one decimal place and money to the nearest pound.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the current maximum output of good units per hour and identify the stage that constrains it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why finishing, which has the lowest stated capacity of the three stages, is not the constraint.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the output of good units per hour under each proposal on its own and under both together, and calculate the cost per additional unit of hourly capacity in each case.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate which proposal, or pair of proposals, Trentvale should approve, using the payback period and two other factors.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Cutting can supply 100 units an hour but machining can process only 90, so the line is throttled to 90 units an hour at machining (M1). Of those, 10% are scrapped, so the good output is 90 × 0.90 = 81 units an hour (A1). Finishing can handle 84 units an hour and receives 81, so it is not full. The maximum output of good units is therefore 81 per hour and the constraint is machining (A1).
**(b)** A stage constrains the line only if the good units arriving at it exceed what it can process. Finishing receives 81 good units an hour and can process 84, so it runs with three units an hour, or 3.6%, of spare capacity (M1)(A1). Its stated capacity is the lowest of the three only because it is quoted before the scrap that happens upstream of it; comparing stated capacities compares the stages at different points in the process, and the comparison that matters is between good units delivered and capacity available at the same point (A1).
**(c)** Proposal 1 alone leaves machining untouched, so output stays at 81 units an hour: the extra finishing capacity is starved and the proposal adds nothing at all (M1). Proposal 2 alone raises good output from machining to 90 × 0.95 = 85.5 units an hour, but finishing can take only 84, so the line delivers 84 units an hour, a gain of 3 units an hour (A1). Both together deliver 85.5 units an hour, a gain of 4.5 units an hour (A1). Cost per additional unit of hourly capacity: Proposal 1, £250 000 for no additional units, so the cost per unit is undefined — no price buys the extra capacity at any level of spending; Proposal 2, £250 000 ÷ 3 = £83 333; both, £500 000 ÷ 4.5 = £111 111, of which the marginal £250 000 buys only 1.5 units an hour, or £166 667 each (A1).
**(d)** Proposal 2 is the one to approve. It adds 3 units an hour, which is 3 × 40 × 48 = 5 760 units a year and 5 760 × £18 = £103 680 of additional contribution, so it pays back in £250 000 ÷ £103 680 = 2.41 years (M1)(A1). Proposal 1 on its own pays back never: it adds no output, so there is no additional contribution against which to recover the £250 000, and it would add depreciation to a stage that already has spare capacity (A1). Two further considerations qualify the recommendation. First, scrap is not only lost output: every scrapped unit has already absorbed £22 of material and machining time, so reducing the scrap rate also improves material productivity and reduces waste disposal, benefits that the contribution calculation does not capture (A1). Second, doing both proposals raises output by a further 1.5 units an hour but costs another £250 000 and stretches payback to 3.21 years; that is worth doing only if Trentvale is confident of selling the extra 8 640 units a year, and demand, not capacity, may then become the constraint (A1).
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for identifying that machining throttles the input to 90 units an hour, (A1) for 81 good units an hour, (A1) for naming machining as the constraint. Accept 81 arrived at as 90 − 9. Do not credit 84 (the lowest stated capacity) or 90 (the lowest stated processing capacity before scrap).
(b) (M1) for the principle that a stage binds only when arrivals exceed its capacity, (A1) for the figures 81 against 84, (A1) for the explanation that the stated capacities are measured at different points in the process. A candidate who says only that 'finishing has spare capacity' without quantifying it earns the first two marks but not the third.
(c) (M1) for recognising that Proposal 1 changes nothing while machining binds, (A1) for 84 units an hour under Proposal 2 with the reason (finishing now binds at 84, not 85.5), (A1) for 85.5 units an hour with both, (A1) for the three cost figures. The cost per unit for Proposal 1 must be stated as undefined or infinite; a candidate who writes £250 000 or zero has not understood the result and loses the mark.
(d) (M1) for converting the extra output into annual units, (A1) for £103 680 and 2.41 years, (A1) for the conclusion that Proposal 1 never pays back, (A1) for one further developed factor such as material productivity, and (A1) for a second, such as the marginal case for doing both or the risk that demand becomes the constraint. Credit the sequencing point — Proposal 1 has value only after Proposal 2 — wherever it appears.
questions.explanation:
Capacity questions invite one move: find the smallest number and call it the bottleneck. This item makes that move wrong in a way that is invisible in the data as presented, because the scrap rate is a property of one stage and its consequence lands on another. Finishing's 84 units an hour is measured in good units arriving; machining's 90 is measured in units started, of which a tenth never arrive. The two numbers are not comparable, and the whole item turns on converting them to a common basis.

The second design decision is to price the error rather than merely expose it. A question that asks only 'which stage is the bottleneck?' can be answered by luck; one that asks what £250 000 spent on the wrong stage buys forces the student to work out that it buys nothing at all — no output, no contribution, and therefore no payback period however long the horizon. That is a stronger and more practical idea than any definition of a bottleneck, and it is the reason the proposals cost the same: with equal price tags, the comparison is purely about what each one releases.

The sequencing result is the last turn. Proposal 1 is worthless alone and worth 1.5 units an hour once Proposal 2 is in place, so the value of a capital project here is not a property of the project but of the order in which it is done — which is exactly the situation the operations syllabus describes and the appraisal syllabus tends to ignore.

provenance.inspired_by: Operations management, the theory of constraints
provenance.adaptation: The source tradition treats the constraint as the resource with the least capacity and teaches the sequence identify–exploit–subordinate–elevate. Here the identification step is made to fail on the textbook's own terms: a scrap rate sits upstream of the stage with the lowest stated capacity, so the constraint is one stage earlier than the numbers suggest, and the elevate step is then priced in two competing currencies so that spending on the wrong stage is shown to buy nothing rather than merely less.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Find the stage with the lowest stated capacity, which is finishing at 84 units an hour, conclude that it is the bottleneck, and approve the proposal that raises its capacity to 110 units an hour.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: Stated capacities are not comparable across stages. Machining's 90 units an hour are units started and a tenth of them are scrapped, so only 81 good units an hour reach a stage that could handle 84; finishing is starved, and the £250 000 spent on it releases nothing, so the wrong design has no cost per unit because it has no units.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The evaluation approves Proposal 1 at a cost of £250 000 and reports a new output of 84 units an hour, when output is already constrained to 81 by machining and the proposal leaves it at 81 — while the same £250 000 spent on the scrap rate would have delivered 84 units an hour and paid back in 2.41 years.

verification.method: Every figure was recomputed in Python. The flow through the line was simulated stage by stage, applying the scrap rate at machining and capping at each stage's capacity, and the output was confirmed to be 81 units an hour under the current settings. All four investment cases were simulated the same way rather than assumed, which is what produced the result that Proposal 1 alone leaves output unchanged and that Proposal 2 alone is capped at 84 by finishing. The payback figures were checked by dividing the investment by the annual contribution and by accumulating contribution year by year, and both routes agree. The figure draws its numbers from the same capacities.
solution_skeleton: convert each stage's stated capacity into good units arriving at the next stage
identify the stage where arrivals first exceed what the stage can process
recompute the flow with each proposal applied alone and with both together
divide each investment by the extra units of hourly capacity it releases
convert the extra output into annual contribution and a payback period
